roadmap.goal: Ship slice 04 of ADO Epic #5775 (Story #5779): an administrator finds out, without writing anything, whether every stored secret is readable and which key each one is on. A read-only pass over every stored secret — including the ones already on the key in force, which is what slice 03's write pass deliberately skips — reports each one in four states that are never collapsed into 'broken': on the key in force, on a key that was retired, in the format this version replaced, and unreadable. Every secret is named by the Connection and the field that own it, so an unreadable one is a thing to go and retype rather than a search. The check works before any rotation has ever run and immediately after one. Separately and unprompted, the encryption settings tell an operator who has just upgraded how many of their secrets are still on the key published with the product, and offer the action that moves them — counted in SQL, so opening the settings page never costs a decrypt of every credential.
roadmap.overview: Five phases, 7 steps, inside-out: the report learns the four states, the traversal learns to look at everything, the route exposes it and the state payload gains the notice count, the panel gains the check and the notice, and the last phase is documentation and the slice close. Slice 03 already shipped the traversal, the report type and the read-only port — this slice widens what the read pass sees and gives it a surface.

slice_to_phase._not_in_this_roadmap_: slices 01-03 (shipped) and slices 05-06 (Stories #5780, #5781) — the Helm chart and the mounted-Secret watcher, and the public docs site pages and security advisory. Narrowing the ring and Encryption:AllowLegacyDefault are recorded as withdrawn in the DISTILL Upstream Issues and are deliberately absent.

phases.name: The four states — what a secret is, rather than what a pass did to it
phases.description: Pure, no I/O. The report slice 03 built counts what a pass did: how many moved, how many could not be read. A check does nothing, so on a check MovedCount is zero by construction and the summary reads as a lie. The four states are what the secret IS, and they are derived from the same record list so a count can never disagree with the list beside it.

steps.name: Four counts that add up to the list they were counted from
steps.description: RED: extend `SecretReadabilityReportTests.cs`. Cases: a secret whose state is readable and whose key id is the active key is counted on the active key; one whose key id is a retired key is counted on an earlier key; a value in the format this version replaced is counted in its own state; an unreadable one is counted as unreadable; the four counts sum to the number of secrets in the list, over an arbitrary mixture; a report over zero records is zero in all four. GREEN: add `OnActiveKeyCount`, `OnRetiredKeyCount` and `PlaintextCount` to `SecretReadabilityReport`, all derived from `Secrets`. No separate total: the list already has a length, and a count that could disagree with it is the defect this type exists to prevent. `UnreadableCount` already exists and is left as it is — an unreadable secret is the only thing that produces the CouldNotBeRead outcome, so the state-based and outcome-based counts are the same number and adding a second one would create the disagreement this type exists to prevent. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): count what each stored secret is, not just what was done to it`.
red_to_green_tests: A readable secret under the active key is counted on the active key
A readable secret under a retired key is counted on an earlier key
A value in the format this version replaced is counted in its own state
An unreadable secret is counted as unreadable and in nothing else
The four counts sum to the number of secrets listed
A report over zero records is zero in all four counts
criteria: Every count is derived from the record list, so the two can never disagree.
No secret is counted twice, and none is left out.

phases.name: The pass that looks at everything
phases.description: Slice 03's candidate predicate is the envelope prefix of the key in force, which is what makes the write pass resumable and idempotent — the database answers what is left to do. Run as a check it returns only what has NOT been done, so a check on a freshly rotated instance reports nothing. The write pass keeps that predicate exactly as it is; the read pass drops it.

steps.name: A check sees every stored secret; a move still sees only what it has work to do on
steps.description: RED: extend `SecretCustodyServiceTests.cs` against the real SQLite context already in that file. Cases: a check on an instance where every secret is on the key in force lists all of them, each with its Connection, its field and the active key id; a check reports a secret on a retired key with that retired key's id; a check names an unreadable secret with the Connection and field that own it; a check leaves every stored value byte for byte (assert over the whole table before and after); two checks in a row report identical counts; a check after a rotation reports every readable secret on the key in force and none on an earlier key; a check on an instance with no stored secrets returns zero secrets and the active key id; the number of database round trips a check makes does not grow with the number of secrets. And the guard on the other side: a re-encryption still visits only the secrets not already on the key in force. GREEN: in `SecretCustodyService`, make the candidate query take a nullable active-key prefix — null for a check, the prefix for a move — and skip the `StartsWith` filter on both the option query and the credential join when it is null. `WalkPastAsync` needs no change: with `moveThem: false` a readable secret is already Unmoved. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): let a check see every stored secret, not only the ones left to move`.
red_to_green_tests: A check lists every stored secret, including the ones already on the key in force
A check names the key each secret is encrypted under, retired keys included
A check names an unreadable secret by its Connection and its field
A check leaves every stored value byte for byte
Two checks in a row report identical counts
A check straight after a rotation reports every readable secret on the key in force
A check on an instance with nothing stored reports zero secrets and the key in force
The number of database round trips does not grow with the number of secrets
A re-encryption still visits only the secrets not already on the key in force
criteria: The check answers 'what is stored', the move answers 'what is left to do', and neither predicate leaks into the other.
Nothing is written by a check, and the thing the check was handed has no way to write.

phases.name: The route, and the count nobody had to ask for
phases.description: One new route, handed the read-only port so it cannot write even by mistake. And one field on the state payload slice 02 already serves, so an operator who opens the settings page is told about the published key without pressing anything and without paying for a decrypt of every credential.

steps.name: GET /encryption/secrets, under the guard already on the controller
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionControllerTests.cs`. Cases: a System Administrator gets the report with every stored secret, each naming its Connection, field, key id and state; nothing in the serialised body is a stored value or a decrypted credential — assert against the raw response text, not against the typed object; a signed-in user who is not a System Administrator is refused and learns nothing about the keys. GREEN: add `[HttpGet("secrets")]` returning `SecretReadabilityReportDto`, taking `ISecretCustodyReader` as its own constructor dependency rather than reusing the service — the check cannot write because of what the controller holds, not because of what it happens to call. Register `ISecretCustodyReader` in the container against the same implementation. No log line: nothing changed, and a record of who read which Connections hold unreadable credentials is the one thing in this feature that would accumulate. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): let a System Administrator check the stored secrets without changing any`.
red_to_green_tests: A System Administrator gets every stored secret with its Connection, field, key and state
Nothing in the serialised body is a stored value or a decrypted credential
A signed-in user who is not a System Administrator is refused
criteria: The route is handed a port with no method that writes.
Nothing that travels to a browser is a credential.

steps.name: How many secrets are still on the key published with the product
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionControllerTests.cs`. Cases: an instance holding secrets under the published key reports that count on the state payload; an instance whose secrets are all on its own key reports zero; an instance with nothing stored reports zero; a value in the format this version replaced — carrying no key id at all — is counted, because that is exactly what an upgraded install holds. GREEN: add a counter over `LighthouseAppContext` that counts, in SQL and without decrypting anything, stored secrets whose value names the published key or predates the envelope format; expose it on `EncryptionStateDto` as `SecretsUnderPublishedKey`. The count is deliberately not a decrypt: an instance that has never rotated would otherwise pay for a full read of every credential each time somebody opens the settings page. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): say how many secrets are still on the key published with the product`.
red_to_green_tests: Secrets under the published key are counted
Values written in the format this version replaced are counted, because an upgraded install holds nothing else
An instance whose secrets are all on its own key counts zero
An instance with nothing stored counts zero
Nothing is decrypted to produce the count
criteria: An operator is told without asking, and without the page paying for a decrypt of every credential.
A fresh install counts zero, so it is never told to fix a problem it does not have.

phases.name: The panel — the check, and the sentence nobody asked for
phases.description: Two things on one screen. The notice is drawn from the state payload, so it is there before anything is pressed. The check is an action, and what it returns is rendered as what IS rather than as what was done — a check that reported 'Moved 0 stored secrets' on a healthy instance would be worse than not asking.

steps.name: The service call, and the model for what comes back
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionService.test.ts`. Cases: `checkSecrets` calls the check route and parses the report; a payload missing a field is rejected by the schema rather than reaching the panel. GREEN: add `checkSecrets()` to `IEncryptionService`/`EncryptionService`, extend `SecretReadabilityReportSchema` with the four counts, and extend `EncryptionKeyStateSchema` with the published-key count. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): fetch what the stored secrets are on`.
red_to_green_tests: checkSecrets asks the check route and returns the parsed report
A payload missing one of the counts is rejected
criteria: The frontend contract and the backend DTO say the same thing, or the schema fails loudly.

steps.name: Check secrets, and the notice beside the action that fixes it
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionPanel.test.tsx`. Cases: an instance with secrets under the published key shows the notice on load, without anything being pressed, naming the count, with the re-encryption action beside it; an instance with zero shows no notice; pressing Check secrets shows how many were checked, how many are on the key in force, how many on an earlier key and how many could not be read; each secret that could not be read is listed with its Connection and its field; a check summary never says anything was moved; a move summary still says what it moved. GREEN: add the notice and the check action to `EncryptionPanel`, and split the summary sentence by which action produced the report. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): show what the stored secrets are on, and say so unprompted`.
red_to_green_tests: The notice is shown on load when secrets are still on the published key, with the count
The re-encryption action is offered beside the notice
No notice is shown when the count is zero
Checking shows the four counts
Each secret that could not be read is listed with its Connection and its field
A check summary never claims anything was moved
A move summary still says what it moved
criteria: An operator who presses nothing still learns their secrets are on a key anyone can obtain.
The remedy is beside the sentence, never a page away.

phases.name: Documentation, mutation testing, slice close
phases.description: The page an operator reads when the check tells them something they did not expect, and the evidence that the tests written above would notice if the code stopped doing what they say.

steps.name: The four states in the docs, Stryker on the changed surface, and the dogfood verdict
steps.description: Extend `docs/Installation/configuration.md` with what the check reports and what an operator does about each of the four states, and with what the published-key notice means. Run Stryker on the changed backend and frontend surface with `stryker-config.epic-5775-slice-04.json`, target >= 80%, and record the run under `docs/feature/epic-5775-secret-encryption-key-custody/mutation/results-5779.md`. Record the flagged taste test's verdict in the slice brief. Dogfood on :5169: check before rotating, corrupt one stored secret, confirm the check names its Connection and field, rotate, confirm the corrupted one is still named while the rest read as being on the key in force. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): say what the check reports and what to do about each state`.
steps.test_file: n/a — documentation, mutation testing and the manual dogfood
steps.scenario_name: Scenarios 96, 97, 98 have no CI substrate; the dogfood is their evidence
criteria: An operator reading the docs knows what to do with each of the four states.
Mutation score >= 80% on the changed surface, on both stacks.
